name: Night of the Living Dead
basisNote: A US film whose copyright lapsed; it is listed among US public domain films.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: Night of the Living Dead (1968)
Wikipedia: films in the public domain in the US

about: A group of strangers barricade themselves inside a farmhouse in rural Pennsylvania while the dead rise and close in from every side. George A. Romero shot it on a tiny budget around Pittsburgh with a cast of unknowns, and it invented the modern zombie film almost by accident: slow, relentless crowds, a siege, and people who turn on each other faster than the monsters do. Duane Jones gives the lead a quiet authority that was rare for a Black actor in a 1968 horror film, and the final scene still lands like a punch. It went out without the copyright notice US law then required, which is why it has been free to watch ever since.
watchIf: you like siege horror, want to see where zombie films began, or have only seen the remakes.

name: Carnival of Souls
basisNote: A US film whose copyright lapsed; it is listed among US public domain films.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: Carnival of Souls (1962)

about: After surviving a car that plunges off a bridge, a church organist moves to a new town in Utah and finds she can't fit back into ordinary life. A pale, grinning man keeps appearing to her, and an abandoned lakeside pavilion seems to be calling her back. Made by an industrial-film director from Kansas with a few thousand dollars, it plays more like a bad dream than a monster movie: long silences, an eerie organ score and faces that look subtly wrong. It flopped on release, then became a cult favourite that directors still name as an influence on everything from Night of the Living Dead to modern indie horror.
watchIf: you like slow, dreamlike horror over jump scares, or you're a fan of The Twilight Zone.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: The Little Shop of Horrors (1960)

about: A clumsy florist's assistant on Skid Row breeds a strange plant to impress the girl he likes, only to find it talks, grows fast and wants human blood. Roger Corman famously shot it in about two days on leftover sets, and the speed shows in the best way: it's loose, deadpan and very funny, with a young Jack Nicholson stealing a scene as a dental patient who enjoys the drill. This is the black-and-white original that later became the stage musical and the 1986 film with the singing plant. The plot is the same story at its rawest, at just over an hour.
watchIf: you know the musical and want the original, or you like low-budget comedy horror.

name: Reefer Madness
basisNote: A US film whose copyright lapsed; it is listed among US public domain films.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: Reefer Madness (1936)
Wikipedia: films in the public domain in the US

about: A high school principal warns parents about a 'new drug menace', then tells the story of clean-cut teenagers lured into a dealer's apartment, where one puff of marijuana leads to hit-and-runs, manic piano playing, madness and murder. It was made as a church-funded warning film in 1936, then sold on to exploitation distributors, and decades later it was rediscovered as unintentional comedy. Watched today it's a time capsule of 1930s moral panic, as interesting for what it gets wrong as for how seriously it takes itself. Short, strange and endlessly quoted, it later inspired a stage musical.
watchIf: you enjoy so-bad-it's-good classics, or you're curious how drug scares were sold in the 1930s.

name: White Zombie
basisNote: A US film whose copyright lapsed; it is listed among US public domain films.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: White Zombie (1932)
Wikipedia: films in the public domain in the US

about: A young couple arrive in Haiti to marry, but a jealous plantation owner makes a deal with a sinister mill owner, played by Bela Lugosi, who controls an army of silent, staring workers raised from the dead. Made a year after Lugosi's most famous role, it's often called the first feature-length zombie film, and its zombies are nothing like Romero's: mindless servants, not flesh-eaters. The pace is slow and stagey, but the images stick, especially the sugar mill scene and Lugosi's hypnotic hand gestures. It draws on William Seabrook's 1929 travel book The Magic Island, itself now out of copyright.
watchIf: you're a Bela Lugosi fan, or you want to see the very first zombie movie.

about: An accountant walks into a Los Angeles police station to report a murder: his own. He has been poisoned, it can't be cured, and he has a day or two to find out who did it and why. Most of the film is that race against the clock, told in flashback, as Edmond O'Brien sweats his way from San Francisco jazz clubs to shady import offices. It has one of the best opening hooks in film noir, real city locations and a sharp, cynical script. A notary's signature on a bill of sale turns out to matter more than anyone could have guessed.
watchIf: you like film noir, mysteries with a ticking clock, or stories told backwards.

about: A star newspaper reporter drops by to tell her editor and ex-husband that she's quitting to marry a mild insurance man. He has other ideas, and a death-row story breaking across the street gives him the perfect excuse to drag her back in. Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell talk over each other at a speed that still feels modern, and Howard Hawks keeps the whole thing moving like a screwball machine. It's routinely named one of the funniest films Hollywood ever made. It was adapted from the 1928 play The Front Page, which is itself now in the public domain.
watchIf: you like fast, witty romantic comedies, or you've never seen a true screwball classic.

Wikipedia: films in the public domain in the US

about: A war crimes investigator, played by Edward G. Robinson, lets a captured Nazi go free in the hope that he will lead him to his former commander. The trail ends in a sleepy Connecticut town, where a respected new schoolteacher, played by Orson Welles, is about to marry the judge's daughter. Welles directed it straight after the war and filled it with shadows, a creepy clock tower and real newsreel footage of the camps, among the first shown in a Hollywood film. It was his biggest hit as a director in his own lifetime, and the cat-and-mouse ending is pure suspense.
watchIf: you like post-war thrillers, Orson Welles, or Hitchcock-style suspense.

about: A young estate agent travels to the Carpathian mountains to sell a house to the strange Count Orlok, who turns out to be a vampire with his eye on the agent's wife back home in Germany. F. W. Murnau's silent film borrowed so heavily from Dracula that Bram Stoker's widow sued and won, and most prints were ordered destroyed. Copies survived, and the film became one of the most influential horror films ever made. Max Schreck's rat-like Orlok, the shadow climbing the stairs and the plague ship drifting into port are images every vampire story since has borrowed from, including the 2024 remake.
watchIf: you liked the 2024 remake, love horror history, or want to try a silent film that still unsettles.

about: A masked figure haunts the cellars beneath the Paris Opera House, coaching a young singer from the shadows and terrorising anyone who stands between her and the lead role. Lon Chaney, the 'man of a thousand faces', designed his own make-up, and the moment the singer pulls off his mask was so shocking in 1925 that cinemas reportedly kept smelling salts on hand. The film is built on Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel, the same story Andrew Lloyd Webber later turned into his musical. The opera house sets, the underground lake and the masked ball sequence are still spectacular a century on.

about: A saintly London doctor, goaded by a cynical friend into wondering about his darker side, invents a potion that splits him in two: the respectable Jekyll and the leering, spider-fingered Hyde. John Barrymore, then America's most celebrated stage actor, performs the first transformation almost entirely with his face and body before the make-up takes over, and it's still startling to watch. The story comes from Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 novella, with a romance added for the screen. It's an early example of a horror film that is really about temptation, and Barrymore's Hyde set the template for every version since.

about: In medieval Paris, the deformed bell-ringer Quasimodo is used by a scheming nobleman to kidnap the street dancer Esmeralda, then humiliated in the square, until she is the only one who shows him kindness. Universal built a full-scale copy of Notre Dame's front for this film, and Lon Chaney put himself through painful make-up and a heavy hump harness to play Quasimodo. It was one of the biggest hits of the silent era and made Chaney a star. The story follows Victor Hugo's 1831 novel, the same one behind the later animated musical, but this version is far darker.

about: A travelling showman arrives at a German fairground with a sleepwalker who, he claims, can predict the future. That night the murders begin. Robert Wiene's film looks like no other: painted sets with crooked streets, slanted windows and shadows drawn straight onto the walls, so the whole town feels like the inside of a disturbed mind. It is the classic example of German Expressionism, and its look runs through Tim Burton films, music videos and modern horror. It also has one of cinema's first great twist endings, which still divides people about what the film is really saying.
watchIf: you like strange visual art, twist endings, or want to see where horror film style began.

evidence.label: Wikipedia: The General (1926)

about: During the American Civil War, a Southern train driver is turned down by the army and dumped by his girlfriend, until Union spies steal his beloved locomotive, with her on board. What follows is one long chase by rail, there and back, with Buster Keaton performing stunts on moving trains that would never be allowed today. He never smiles, and he never needs to. The comedy comes from perfect timing and enormous physical risk, and the bridge collapse near the end used a real train. Critics now rank it among the greatest comedies ever made, though it flopped in 1926.
watchIf: you like action comedy, daring stunts, or want a silent film that's genuinely fun.

about: A London estate agent named Renfield travels to Transylvania to close a property deal with Count Dracula, and comes home as the count's raving servant. Dracula follows him to England, where he moves into a ruined abbey and begins preying on the young women next door, until the vampire expert Van Helsing works out who he is. Bela Lugosi had played the role on Broadway, and his slow voice, cape and stare became the image of the vampire for the next century. The film is based on the stage play adapted from Bram Stoker's 1897 novel, and both are now in the public domain.

about: A young scientist, Henry Frankenstein, shuts himself away in a watchtower to build a man from body parts and bring him to life with lightning. It works, but the creature he has made is given a criminal's brain, rejected and chained up, and his escape ends in tragedy for everyone. James Whale's film is short and moves fast, and Boris Karloff, under heavy make-up, makes the monster frightening and pitiful at once without a word of dialogue. The story comes from Peggy Webling's 1927 stage play based on Mary Shelley's 1818 novel, all of which are now in the public domain.
watchIf: you want the most famous monster film of all, or you only know the creature from parodies.
